A 1776 monument commissioned for diplomacy is being retooled as a weapon against democratic memory.

America’s First Monument
Evidence: Pure Martial Glory, Partisan Culture War, Democratic Civic Remembrance
#Aletheia #History 🌐

The Washington Examiner claims the 1776 Montgomery monument proves true commemoration must focus strictly on battlefield combat, attacking modern memorials for honoring civilian democracy and homefront sacrifice.

Stated Judgement: (+0.96, +1.00) — Greater Good

Franklin commissioned the 1776 monument in Paris for diplomatic alliance, using Enlightenment symbols of liberty. Honoring citizen-soldiers and civilian mobilization upholds republican democracy over martial idolatry.

Resulting Judgement: (-0.16, +0.23) — Greatest Lie

Verdict: FAIL — Fall into Deception.
The column weaponizes early American art to delegitimize democratic remembrance, erasing the citizen-soldier ideal to stoke culture-war division.

Integrity: Meaningful Distortion (Hypocrisy: 7.80, z: 3)

- Washington Examiner: FAIL (-0.71, +0.62) — Distorts 1776 history into culture war.
- Fox News: FAIL (-0.68, -0.45) — Partisan SBA fraud spin misclustered in topic.
- Civic Remembrance: PASS (+0.85, +0.70) — Honors citizen-soldiers and democracy.

The Washington Examiner celebrated America’s first commissioned monument—honoring Gen. Richard Montgomery at St. Paul’s Chapel—while condemning modern memorials for recognizing collective civilian and homefront contributions during World War II.

The Bright Side:
Rediscovering the Montgomery Monument highlights the stunning craftsmanship of Jean-Jacques Caffieri and the rich, complex diplomatic history of Benjamin Franklin securing French backing during the Revolution.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
This is a WHAT vs WHO error, confusing classical baroque aesthetic with democratic purpose. The bait honors a fallen general; the switch devalues the millions of citizen-soldiers and civilians whose collective labor secured victory in WWII.

Social Physics Analysis:
The commentator executes a Smart Selfish maneuver. The secret goal is manufacturing partisan resentment; the pretext is defending martial honor; the projection accuses democratic memorials of political correctness for honoring citizen-soldiers.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Deception.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Lesser Evil. Elevating Spartan martial dominance over democratic solidarity collapses civic trust into cynicism.

The Unavoidable Truth: American democracy is defended by citizen-soldiers, making total national mobilization worthy of civic honor.

The Unavoidable Lie: Honoring collective civilian and logistical sacrifice somehow demeans the combat troops who fought.

Alethekanon:
Monuments in a republic exist to anchor civic virtue, not to sanctify a permanent warrior caste. Erasing the citizen from the soldier converts democratic gratitude into authoritarian aesthetics.

Awwthekanon:
Every life given in war represents an irreplaceable loss, whether in 1775 or 1944. True honor does not pit the front lines against the mothers, machinists, and medics who sustained them; it holds all who carried the burden in shared grace.

Brothekanon:
Imagine looking at the WWII Memorial and getting mad that it honors the whole country pulling together instead of just glorifying blood and guts. Ike literally warned us about military worship, but pundits gotta culture-war everything.

Spirithekanon:
"The eye cannot say to the hand, 'I have no need of you,' nor the head to the feet, 'I have no need of you.'" 1 Corinthians 12:21 FAIL
Commemoration that elevates the fighter while disparaging the civilian homefront fractures the shared civic body.

[Source 1 — www.washingtonexaminer.com] (URL: https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/restoring-america/patriotism-unity/4764198/montgomery-monument-honoring-warriors-american-history/):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
America’s first monument is a lesson in how to honor our warriors

In 1776, for the country’s first act of commemoration, the Continental Congress shipped Benjamin Franklin off to Paris with 300 pounds sterling for the proposed Gen. Richard Montgomery monument. Actual Article Body:
Conservative values, National renewal

In 1776, for the country’s first act of commemoration, the Continental Congress shipped Benjamin Franklin off to Paris with 300 pounds sterling for the proposed Gen. Richard Montgomery monument. Franklin hired Jean-Jacques Caffieri, and, under his chisel, the marble grew into an altar overflowing with Greco-Roman and Biblical symbols. The monument now decorates the facade of St. Paul’s Chapel, a short walk from the World Trade Center site.

Flowering amid the Revolutionary War, the Montgomery Memorial is an essential lesson in celebrating our own warriors, a lavish illustration of the personal sacrifice and transcendent accomplishment that define war. Such high deeds command our honor, and honor itself depends upon their just retelling.

Join Washington Examiner for unlimited access to the news, analysis, and commentary that matter most.

Already a member? Log in

Gen. Montgomery had been a captain in the British army but later resigned, eventually joining the Revolutionary War to defend the rights of the colonies. Montgomery died from cannon fire in Quebec in 1775 while leading a hopelessly small group of men in a snowstorm-drowned battle. Completed in France, his memorial crossed the Atlantic Ocean in the melee of war, resting in limbo for eight years inside its boxes at the port of Edenton, North Carolina.

Congressional delegate Charles DeWitt, of New York, proposed St. Paul’s Chapel as the monument’s final resting site: a matchbox-sized but stately Colonial church on an island of graveyard green. Around 1788, the monument went up outside the church, at the base of its central window. Pierre L’Enfant, later the city planner of Washington, D.C., designed the gold-and-white relief sculpture that conceals the dark outline seen from inside the chapel, a billowing baroque scene depicting the Shekinah glory of God and the Ten Commandments. A painted panel on the upper reverse side envisions the new nation as a dawning sun with 13 rays.

An inscription below the memorial outside the church, full of affinity for capitalization, explains that “This Monument is erected by the order of Congress 25th Jan. 1776 to transmit to Posterity a grateful remembrance of the patriotism conduct enterprise & perseverance of Major General Richard Montgomery. Who after a series of successes amidst the most discouraging Difficulties Fell in the attack on QUEBEC. 31st Dec 1775. Aged 37 Years.”

Montgomery was patriotic, he fought relentlessly, and he was full of enterprise and persistence. “Enterprise” means “bold action.” Like a Greek oration, the words set a glowing scene of the general’s good deeds and inner life, keeping with the commission by Congress. The monument, the commission expressed, was to display “veneration” for the fallen soldier and his “insuperable perseverance and contempt of danger and death.” These qualities were to be on display for all “future ages, as examples truly worthy of imitation.”

Sacrifice and remarkable achievement, the sculpture’s two main themes, organize the design of the monument. A funerary obelisk and a cut column crowned by an urn divide heaps of symbols: the first set of carvings is elegiac, representing a military death. Here rests a cypress branch, the Roman symbol of respect for the dead, and a helmet, armor, and flags — a grouping of armor called a trophee d’armes. A broken sword slid under the breastplate announces a hero’s life cut short. The urn, sword, and cypress speak almost as clearly as they might have in 1777: a warrior has given the greatest sacrifice, they intone, make no mistake.

If one side of the monument conveys that a warrior has died, the other shows what he fought and died for. A soft liberty cap and pole, symbols of the Revolution, and a Herculean club, emerge from the bowing leaves of a palm. A stiff banner wraps the club in the phrase “libertas restituta,” an injunction translated as “restore liberty.” Two mysterious objects tilt at the foot of the club: the shattered bar of an oxen yoke, the yoke of tyranny described in Isaiah 58:6, the tyranny of a despot.

When Franklin commissioned the sculpture in 1777, American victory was still in the offing, six years distant, a hope appearing blue and phantasmagorical to the imaginations of the fighting rebels. Still, the symbols of the monument crystallize the causes of the rebellion, explaining Montgomery’s role and motivation, and the inscription below the memorial recalls his personal achievements — a string of victorious battles.

Notably, every carefully chosen detail of the Montgomery Monument alludes to one or both of its twin main themes. This is no accident. Inseparable complementary aspects frame war: unfathomable sacrifice and superlative achievement. It is these that command our honor and justify our commemoration.

Because the memorial is located in the city just steps away from another story of sacrifice, its values shine brightly. Sacrifice and heroic deeds seem relevant, relatable. In our contemporary memorials, however, we have forgotten the importance of such themes. For decades, monument architects have minimized representations of suffering and obfuscated accomplishment. Consumed by political correctness, memorials have become vague and noncommittal, both elaborate and evasive, formless and empty.

The 2020 Washington, D.C., Dwight D. Eisenhower Memorial begins, unaccountably, at boyhood in Abilene, Kansas. The general’s greatest achievement, that of unimaginable victory, is played down, overshadowed by the three-part biographical narrative telling “the quintessential American story.” Victory palms and Nike alighting on a warship are only to be dreamt of. Even as Eisenhower’s Homecoming Speech, included in the monument, praises the value of honor — the “dreams of a barefoot boy” — the National Park Service description demurs, disavowing such an outdated ideal and declaring hyperbolically that “Eisenhower returned to his hometown” of Abilene “as not the leader of the forces that helped to defeat Nazi Germany but as another citizen.”

Then there is the 2004 World War II Memorial on the National Mall, a design that erodes the traditional theme of highest sacrifice through combat with a broad premise honoring the contributions of an entire country. “Virtually everyone supported the war,” the 123-page brief published by the NPS assures us, “and worked to achieve victory.”

Fifty-six pillars inscribed with the states and territories consume the greatest space, and the sacrifice of more than 400,000 American men who gave their lives in history’s bloodiest war is relegated to a smaller commemorative area of 4,048 stars. Why the entire monument is not gold stars is left for the visitor to ponder before the monument’s rushing fountains. Removing combat from its traditional dominance strips honor from those most needful of it, handing it instead to arbitrary role groups, and the design obscures the very sacrifices justifying the existence of the memorial.

WHY WASHINGTON’S MOST MAGNIFICENT MONUMENTS BARELY MADE IT ON THE MAP

History has many pages, it is true. The facts will always be many. Justice, on the other hand, is narrow and stringent, sharply pointed and exact. Honor is paid through a symmetrical retelling; when we dilute the light of sacrifice and achievement, symmetry is lost, and justice scatters.

We must choose one of two pains: the pain of honor or the pain of its dismemberment — there are no other alternatives. The Montgomery memorial, richly decorated and compact, establishes a high precedent of acclaim. Its warrior’s legacy bursts into bright light, an eternal remembrance of the first American officer to die for his country. Like 13 rays of a rising sun, the monument illuminates our way forward in enacting justice for veterans, serves as a standard for all ages, and is an emblem of sacrifice and achievement.

Amanda Johnson is a writer whose work on commemoration and civic art has appeared in National Review. Read more at amandajohnsonwriter.com.

The SBA suspended 870,000 borrowers linked to an estimated $39 billion in suspected pandemic loan fraud, the largest action in agency history.

Republican strategist Mehek Cooke says the Biden administration's laws left room for rampant fraud on ‘Fox Report.’

As the White House's Fraud Ledger shows, the Small Business Administration (SBA) has uncovered more fraud than any other agency. Through Vice President JD Vance's Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, the Trump administration is eliminating waste, fraud and abuse at historic rates.

When COVID shut down the country, small business owners did everything they could to keep their doors open. They drained their savings, skipped paychecks, and fought to keep employees on the payroll.

While small businesses were fighting to survive, fraudsters stole billions from programs meant to keep them afloat. The Biden-Harris administration had years to hold fraudsters accountable. It never did. Under Republican leadership, that era is over.

WHITE HOUSE LAUNCHES INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD

Last month, SBA Administrator Kelly Loeffler stood with Vice President Vance in Kansas City, Missouri, and announced the suspension of 870,000 borrowers linked to an estimated $39 billion in suspected pandemic fraud, the largest action of its kind in the agency's history.

As chairman of the House Committee on Small Business, I've worked closely with Administrator Loeffler to go after this money and ensure Main Street isn't left high and dry. Every dollar a fraudster took was a dollar a family business didn't get.

The Biden-Harris SBA knew COVID fraud was rampant and still failed to act. In 2023, the SBA’s Office of Inspector General estimated that more than $200 billion in pandemic loans may have gone to fraudsters. Agency leadership at the time stated the actual number was closer to $36 billion.

When our committee asked then-SBA Administrator Isabella Guzman to explain the $164 billion difference, she refused to testify. So we kept digging.

WHITE HOUSE PUSHES 'WATERSHED' FRAUD-FIGHTING REFORM IN CONGRESS AS VANCE CONVENES TASK FORCE

Our committee spent 18 months investigating the pandemic loan programs. What we found was deeply disturbing. Rather than fixing its own broken controls, Biden's SBA pointed fingers at the private lenders it worked with. It even floated ending collections on fraudulent loans under $100,000, valued at about $11 billion, because it didn't want to appear to be strong-arming borrowers.

Unfortunately, pandemic loans aren't the whole story.

Just look at the 8(a) program, which helps disadvantaged small businesses compete for federal contracts. It only works if those firms do the work themselves. Pass-through schemes, in which the winning firm hands the job off to someone else, cheat the very businesses the program was meant to help.

In an effort to rein in fraudulent spending, Administrator Loeffler did something nobody had done in nearly 50 years: she audited the entire program. When hundreds of firms refused to hand over their financial records, she moved to kick them out. The SBA has also closed loopholes that let loans be issued in the names of children and the deceased, some of whom are listed as being older than 115.

House Republicans have helped lead this recovery from the start, and are ensuring these reforms stick. In June, the House passed my COVID Fraud Transparency Act, which requires the SBA's inspector general to report quarterly to Congress on COVID loan fraud. My committee also advanced pragmatic anti-fraud bills, including Republican Pennsylvania Rep. Dan Meuser's Small Business Lending Fraud Prevention Act and my bipartisan Put America on Commission Act.

I've spent my career in the car business, and I know that paying commissions delivers results. My bill, the Put America on Commission Act, would reward Americans who come forward with credible tips about pandemic loan fraud, funded by penalties paid by convicted fraudsters.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

When I became chairman, I said we would not write this money off. Democrats spent four years ignoring this fraud and were ready to forgive billions of dollars. House Republicans, alongside Administrator Loeffler and Vice President Vance, will continue pursuing it so that the next time mom-and-pop shops need help, they won't have to stand in line behind fraudsters.

Republican Roger Williams represents the 25th Congressional District of Texas, which includes Fort Hood, in the U.S. House of Representatives.

We must choose one of two pains: the pain of honor or the pain of its dismemberment — there are no other alternatives. The Montgomery memorial, richly decorated and compact, establishes a high precedent of acclaim. Its warrior’s legacy bursts into bright light, an eternal remembrance of the first American officer to die for his country. Like 13 rays of a rising sun, the monument illuminates our way forward in enacting justice for veterans, serves as a standard for all ages, and is an emblem of sacrifice and achievement.

Amanda Johnson is a writer whose work on commemoration and civic art has appeared in National Review. Read more at amandajohnsonwriter.com.

As the White House's Fraud Ledger shows, the Small Business Administration (SBA) has uncovered more fraud than any other agency. Through Vice President JD Vance's Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, the Trump administration is eliminating waste, fraud and abuse at historic rates.

When COVID shut down the country, small business owners did everything they could to keep their doors open. They drained their savings, skipped paychecks, and fought to keep employees on the payroll.

While small businesses were fighting to survive, fraudsters stole billions from programs meant to keep them afloat. The Biden-Harris administration had years to hold fraudsters accountable. It never did. Under Republican leadership, that era is over.

WHITE HOUSE LAUNCHES INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD

Last month, SBA Administrator Kelly Loeffler stood with Vice President Vance in Kansas City, Missouri, and announced the suspension of 870,000 borrowers linked to an estimated $39 billion in suspected pandemic fraud, the largest action of its kind in the agency's history.

As chairman of the House Committee on Small Business, I've worked closely with Administrator Loeffler to go after this money and ensure Main Street isn't left high and dry. Every dollar a fraudster took was a dollar a family business didn't get.

The Biden-Harris SBA knew COVID fraud was rampant and still failed to act. In 2023, the SBA’s Office of Inspector General estimated that more than $200 billion in pandemic loans may have gone to fraudsters. Agency leadership at the time stated the actual number was closer to $36 billion.

When our committee asked then-SBA Administrator Isabella Guzman to explain the $164 billion difference, she refused to testify. So we kept digging.

WHITE HOUSE PUSHES 'WATERSHED' FRAUD-FIGHTING REFORM IN CONGRESS AS VANCE CONVENES TASK FORCE

Our committee spent 18 months investigating the pandemic loan programs. What we found was deeply disturbing. Rather than fixing its own broken controls, Biden's SBA pointed fingers at the private lenders it worked with. It even floated ending collections on fraudulent loans under $100,000, valued at about $11 billion, because it didn't want to appear to be strong-arming borrowers.

Unfortunately, pandemic loans aren't the whole story.

Just look at the 8(a) program, which helps disadvantaged small businesses compete for federal contracts. It only works if those firms do the work themselves. Pass-through schemes, in which the winning firm hands the job off to someone else, cheat the very businesses the program was meant to help.

In an effort to rein in fraudulent spending, Administrator Loeffler did something nobody had done in nearly 50 years: she audited the entire program. When hundreds of firms refused to hand over their financial records, she moved to kick them out. The SBA has also closed loopholes that let loans be issued in the names of children and the deceased, some of whom are listed as being older than 115.

House Republicans have helped lead this recovery from the start, and are ensuring these reforms stick. In June, the House passed my COVID Fraud Transparency Act, which requires the SBA's inspector general to report quarterly to Congress on COVID loan fraud. My committee also advanced pragmatic anti-fraud bills, including Republican Pennsylvania Rep. Dan Meuser's Small Business Lending Fraud Prevention Act and my bipartisan Put America on Commission Act.

I've spent my career in the car business, and I know that paying commissions delivers results. My bill, the Put America on Commission Act, would reward Americans who come forward with credible tips about pandemic loan fraud, funded by penalties paid by convicted fraudsters.
